In this wisdom psalm, the psalmist: 

- asks for healing ({{Psalm 41:4|Psalm 41:4}}, {{Psalm 41:10|10}}),

- laments his distress ({{Psalm 41:5-9|Psalm 41:5–9}}), and

- expresses confidence in the Lord's blessing ({{Psalm 41:1-3|Psalm 41:1–3}}, {{Psalm 41:11-12|11–12}}).

*on his bed of illness*: This illness might be physical or spiritual (see {{Psalm 6:2|Psalm 6:2}}; {{Psalm 38:1-22|Psalm 38}}).

The psalmist applies the blessing to himself ({{Psalm 41:12|Psalm 41:12}}). He has helped the poor ({{Psalm 41:1|Psalm 41:1}}), but he has sinned against the Lord in other ways. In his pain, he asks for healing and admits his sin. Only the Lord can provide the restoration that brings true joy ({{Psalm 30:2|Psalm 30:2}}; {{Psalm 107:20-21|107:20–21}}).
T
*When will he die*: The psalmist's enemies see his suffering as a judgment from God (see {{Psalm 1:6|Psalm 1:6}}).
T
The psalmist’s enemies disguise themselves as friends, while his friends openly become his enemies.
T

*the one who shared my bread*: Eating together was a sign of unity ({{Acts 2:42|Acts 2:42}}). Refusing to eat with someone was a sign of hostility ({{1 Corinthians 5:11|1 Corinthians 5:11}}). Jesus experienced the same kind of betrayal ({{John 13:1|John 13:1}}, {{John 13:18|18}}).
T
The psalmist knows that the Lord has forgiven him and will bless him.

The sons of Korah were members of a Levitical choir. They were chosen by David to serve as singers in the temple (see {{1 Chronicles 6:22-38|1 Chronicles 6:22–38}}; {{1 Chronicles 9:19-34|9:19–34}}; {{2 Chronicles 20:19|2 Chronicles 20:19}}). Their ancestor Korah was the rebel who opposed Moses and was swallowed by the earth ({{Exodus 6:24|Exodus 6:24}}; {{Numbers 16:1-50|Numbers 16}}).
T

- The psalmist's deep desire for God arises from being far away from the temple as he remembers the past. 

- The verb translated as "longs" appears only here and in {{Joel 1:20|Joel 1:20}} (meaning "cry out"). In both instances, it describes extreme thirst in a dry desert (see {{Psalm 63:1|Psalms 63:1}}; {{Psalm 143:6|143:6}}; see also {{Psalm 84:2|84:2}}).
T

These psalms, like {{Psalm 9:1-20|Psalms 9}} and {{Psalm 10:1-18|10}}, form a unit with a lament and a bittersweet refrain of hope ({{Psalm 42:5|Psalm 42:5}}, {{Psalm 42:11|11}}; {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}). Many Hebrew manuscripts combine these two psalms into one. 

The historical context is unclear; these psalms might represent God's people in exile, expressing loyalty to God while he punishes them for their ongoing disobedience. 

The psalmist longs for the fellowship with God he had in Jerusalem ({{Psalm 42:4|Psalm 42:4}}); his memories only deepen his discouragement. As the psalmist cries out to God, he remembers God's love and faithfulness ({{Psalm 42:8|Psalm 42:8}}), which leads him to ask for vindication ({{Psalm 43:1-4|43:1–4}}).
T

- Crying so much that tears become food shows deep sadness ({{Psalm 80:5|Psalms 80:5}}; {{Psalm 102:9|102:9}}; see {{Psalm 6:6|6:6}}; {{Psalm 56:8|56:8}}; {{Psalm 119:136|119:136}}; {{Psalm 126:5|126:5}}). 

- The wicked try to impose their timing on God and deny his power to intervene.
T
The psalmist remembers leading a large procession as part of the Levitical choir, possibly during the important holy days.
T
The psalmist feels sad, but he can still function. He remembers that the living God is his Savior. This verse appears again in {{Psalm 42:11|Psalms 42:11}} and {{Psalm 43:5|43:5}}.
T
The psalmist encourages himself with questions and answers.
T

- Mount Mizar might be a peak in the Mount Hermon range.

The raging seas, waves, and surging tides bring to mind God's anger (see {{Psalm 88:7|Psalm 88:7}}).
T
The psalmist sees rays of hope. A life focused on God includes joyful songs and prayers for justice and vindication ({{Psalm 42:9-10|Psalm 42:9–10}}; {{Psalm 43:1-4|43:1–4}}).
T
The psalmist brings his many doubts, discouragements, and questions directly to God.
T
The psalmist turns to the Lord for rescue from his troubles, for guidance, for restoration, and for vindication.

- The temple on the mountain in Jerusalem symbolized God's holy presence among his people ({{Psalm 15:1|Psalms 15:1}}; {{Psalm 43:3|43:3}}; {{Psalm 99:5|99:5}}, {{Psalm 99:9|9}}; {{Psalm 132:7|132:7}}).

This national lament after a defeat in battle continues the tone of the previous two psalms. It reflects on an unspecified moment in Israel's history and calls on God for salvation. The people: 

- recite God's past acts of rescue ({{Psalm 44:1-3|Psalm 44:1–3}}),

- recognize God's power to save ({{Psalm 44:4-8|Psalm 44:4–8}}),

- describe their humiliation in exile ({{Psalm 44:9-16|Psalm 44:9–16}}),

- claim their innocence and lament the injustice of their current situation ({{Psalm 44:17-22|Psalm 44:17–22}}), and

- cry for vindication ({{Psalm 44:23-26|Psalm 44:23–26}}).

God drove out the pagan nations during the conquests recorded in Joshua.

This psalm celebrates a royal wedding; it might have been sung on many occasions and not just at one wedding. As God’s representative, the king carried the responsibility of dispensing justice and maintaining order in God’s world (see {{Psalm 2:1-12|Psalm 2}}).

This general description of the king’s symbolic status anticipates his enduring legacy ({{Psalm 45:16|Psalm 45:16}}). The Lord’s blessing and the charge to reflect God’s attributes are symbolized by his handsome appearance and gracious speech.

Glory and majesty belong to the Lord ({{Psalm 96:6|Psalms 96:6}}; {{Psalm 111:3|111:3}}).

The psalmist describes the royal splendor the king showed when fighting his enemies.

As God's representative of truth, humility, and justice (see {{Psalm 72:1-2|Psalm 72:1–2}}, {{Psalm 72:4|4}}, {{Psalm 72:7|7}}), the king can perform impressive deeds ({{Psalm 65:5|65:5}}; {{Psalm 96:4|96:4}}).

Justice characterizes God’s rule, as it should characterize the king’s administration.

- The king is like a god among humans. God anointed him, gave him a powerful throne, and he delivers justice as he rules eternally. 

- The writer of Hebrews uses {{Psalm 45:6-7|Psalm 45:6–7}} to describe Jesus, arguing that the Son is greater than the angels ({{Hebrews 1:8-9|Hebrews 1:8–9}}).

- *know that I am God*: The Lord will fulfill his promises ({{Isaiah 45:3|Isaiah 45:3}}; {{Isaiah 49:23|49:23}}; {{Isaiah 60:16|60:16}}). 

- God will be honored ({{Psalm 47:1-9|Psalm 47}}; {{Isaiah 6:1|Isaiah 6:1}}); he will judge the nations and save his people (see {{Psalm 57:11|Psalms 57:11}}; {{Psalm 89:13|89:13}}; {{Psalm 108:5-6|108:5–6}}; {{Psalm 118:16|118:16}}).

People clap their hands in praise and recognition of wonderful deeds ({{Psalm 47:3-4|Psalm 47:3–4}}; see {{Psalm 98:8|98:8}}; {{Isaiah 55:12|Isaiah 55:12}}; compare {{Nahum 3:19|Nahum 3:19}}).
T
As the ruler of all nations, God deserves praise.
T

This psalm praises God's rule as king over the entire earth. It describes God's victory with Israel and other nations. Both Israel ({{Psalm 47:3-4|Psalm 47:3–4}}) and the nations ({{Psalm 47:9|47:9}}) are part of God's kingdom.
T
The Lord gave Israel victory, especially under David (see {{Psalm 18:40-50|Psalm 18:40–50}}). God's powerful acts of redemption show his love for Israel.
T

- *pride of Jacob*: Jacob was the father of all Israelites ({{Genesis 32:28|Genesis 32:28}}). The name *Jacob* often represents the nation of Israel. 

- God loves and commits himself to Jacob (see {{Psalm 78:68|Psalms 78:68}}; {{Psalm 127:2|127:2}}; see {{Romans 11:28|Romans 11:28}}).
T

*horn*: Or *rams’ horns* (see {{Psalm 81:3|Psalm 81:3}}). People sometimes blew rams’ horns during celebrations ({{Psalm 98:5-6|Psalm 98:5–6}}; {{2 Kings 11:14|2 Kings 11:14}}; {{1 Chronicles 15:28|1 Chronicles 15:28}}).
T
The psalmist describes the Lord as returning to heaven, having accomplished his victories. For a description of his descent, see {{Psalm 18:9-16|Psalm 18:9–16}}.
T
People from all over the world (see {{Psalm 96:1-3|Psalm 96:1–3}}) will worship God.
T

This song of Zion (see also {{Psalm 46:1-11|Psalms 46}}, {{Psalm 76:1-12|76}}, {{Psalm 87:1-7|87}}, {{Psalm 122:1-9|122}}) clearly describes Jerusalem (Zion) as the city of the Great King, where the godly find protection ({{Psalm 48:1-3|48:1–3}}). God rules from Zion with faithfulness, righteousness, and justice, inspiring his people with confidence and joy ({{Psalm 48:9-11|Psalm 48:9–11}}). They dedicate themselves to witnessing Zion's glory so they can share it with the next generation ({{Psalm 48:8|Psalm 48:8}}, {{Psalm 48:12-14|12–14}}).
T
God lives in Zion to protect it from all enemies (see {{Psalm 46:5|Psalm 46:5}}).
T

The ships of Tarshish were built for long voyages and represent human achievement (see also {{2 Chronicles 9:21|2 Chronicles 9:21}}; {{Isaiah 2:16|Isaiah 2:16}}). Their destruction might be the event mentioned in {{1 Kings 22:48|1 Kings 22:48}}.
T
The psalmist happily celebrates the Lord's presence with the community, thinking about God's faithful, righteous, and just rule.
T
*towers … ramparts … citadel*: These structures show Zion's strength.
T

No one is like God ({{Psalm 35:10|Psalms 35:10}}; {{Psalm 71:19|71:19}}; {{Psalm 86:8|86:8}}; {{Psalm 89:6|89:6}}, {{Psalm 89:8|8}}; {{Psalm 113:5|113:5}}; see {{Isaiah 40:18|Isaiah 40:18}}, {{Isaiah 40:25|25}}). He is the shepherd King ({{Psalm 95:7|Psalm 95:7}}) who will guide (see {{Psalm 5:8|5:8}}; {{Psalm 23:2|23:2}}) the sheep of his flock ({{Psalm 77:20|77:20}}).
T
Anyone who will listen can gain wisdom ({{Proverbs 1:5|Proverbs 1:5}}, {{Proverbs 1:8|8}}, {{Proverbs 1:33|33}}).
T
The wisdom teacher invites everyone to come and learn wisdom. He promises to teach them through a proverb and a riddle.
T

In this wisdom psalm, a wise teacher warns about enemies who live richly and care only for themselves ({{Psalm 49:5-9|Psalm 49:5–9}}). They cannot save anyone, not even themselves, from death or being forgotten ({{Psalm 49:10-12|Psalm 49:10–12}}). Like fattened animals, they are led to slaughter ({{Psalm 49:14-20|Psalm 49:14–20}}).
T
The teacher used proverbs and riddles to teach wisdom (see {{Proverbs 1:5-6|Proverbs 1:5–6}}).
T
If enemies who live for material rewards cannot sustain themselves, how can they give life to others?
T
The teacher uses irony to teach wisdom. Everyone dies, and even those who give their names to lands or estates will be forgotten.
T
The teachers of false wisdom cannot rescue themselves from death. Only God has that power.
T
The wicked might have rich, luxurious lives, but they forget that they cannot avoid death.
T
The whole universe must pay attention when God approaches to bring justice into the world.
T
God appears as judge. He reminds both the godly and the ungodly that sacrifices and reciting the law are worthless without thankfulness, repentance, and justice.
T

The Lord is coming to bring justice. This hope encourages his faithful people. However, those who have been unfaithful will not receive blessings when the heavens and earth testify against them (see {{Deuteronomy 30:19|Deuteronomy 30:19}}; {{Deuteronomy 31:28|31:28}}; {{Deuteronomy 32:1|32:1}}; {{Isaiah 1:2|Isaiah 1:2}}). The Lord comes to restore order to the world (see {{Psalm 5:8|Psalms 5:8}}; {{Psalm 22:31|22:31}}; {{Psalm 33:5|33:5}}; {{Psalm 40:9|40:9}}; {{Psalm 50:6|50:6}}; {{Psalm 71:16|71:16}}; {{Psalm 97:6|97:6}}).
T
The psalmist warns against valuing sacrificial rituals more than having the right attitude in your heart.
T
Unlike pagan gods, God does not need food. Instead, he wants his people to serve him with sincere hearts ({{Psalm 50:14-15|Psalm 50:14–15}}).
T
*the cattle on a thousand hills*: God has no needs because he owns everything.
T

- Thankfulness involves recognizing and appreciating God's blessings beyond personal gain (see {{Psalm 51:15-17|Psalms 51:15–17}}; {{Psalm 54:6|54:6}}). 

- True sacrifice means dedicating oneself to honor God ({{Psalm 50:23|Psalm 50:23}}; {{Romans 12:1-2|Romans 12:1–2}}).
T
God’s response to his people’s cry is to rescue them.
T
This message is against the wicked, who only pretend to listen to God.
T
*My instruction … My words*: The wicked may observe rituals, but they reject more important matters such as justice, mercy, and faithfulness (compare {{Matthew 23:23-24|Matthew 23:23–24}}).
T
Because he is patient, God remained silent.
T
God will destroy the wicked like a lion tearing its prey ({{Isaiah 5:29|Isaiah 5:29}}; {{Isaiah 31:4|31:4}}; {{Ezekiel 19:3|Ezekiel 19:3}}; compare {{Psalm 7:2|Psalms 7:2}}; {{Psalm 22:13|22:13}}).
T
The wicked will experience God’s justice, while the godly will see God’s everlasting salvation.
